$comment: On-chain alert definitions for Tosh v5.0. Consumed by monitoring/watch.mjs and
validated by scripts/verifyAlertTopics.js.
There is no `$schema` key. This file used to declare one pointing at
./alerts.schema.md, which has never existed — a dangling reference that looked
like validation and was not. The real check is scripts/verifyAlertTopics.js.
Each alert carries either `event` + `topic0` (log subscription) or `check`
(scheduled state read), plus `severity`, `page`, and a `why` stating what the
alert is actually evidence of. `playbook` carries the response inline, or names
tosh-status/MANUAL_INTERACTION.md for the steps users are walked through, or is
null where the alert is an audit trail with no response to run.
NOTE: verifyAlertTopics.js validates events and topic0 against the compiled
ABIs, and now also fails on any playbook or action naming a repo file that is
not on disk. It drifted twice before that check existed: eleven playbooks once
pointed at the wrong section, and later every one of them pointed at an
incident doc that had been deleted. Prose in this file is still unchecked.
Deliberately provider-neutral. Every commercial monitor (OpenZeppelin Defender,
Tenderly, Hypernative, a self-hosted log subscriber) can express 'topic0 == X on
address Y', and none of them agree on a config format. Encoding the intent here
and translating at import time means the reviewable artifact is this file rather
than someone's dashboard screenshot.
`topic0` values are verified against the compiled ABIs by
scripts/verifyAlertTopics.js, which runs in CI. They cannot silently drift from
the contracts.
GOV-05 IS GONE, ON PURPOSE. It watched TreasuryUpdated(address), the companion
event to setPlatformTreasury. Both were deleted when platformTreasury went back
onto a money path — it now takes 0.30 % of the BEM input of every buy — because a
mutable fee-routing target is audit finding M-2, so the mutability went rather
than the inflow. The field is immutable on the factory and the same address is
baked into the hook implementation as platformFeeRecipient. The event can
therefore never fire again, and a rule that can never fire is silent for the
wrong reason: indistinguishable, on a dashboard, from a healthy system. Nothing
replaces it as a governance watch, because there is no longer a governance action
to watch — the address cannot be retargeted by anyone, including the owner. The
fee flow itself is observable via ToshLaunchpadHook.PlatformSwapFeePaid, which is
per-buy and therefore classified under mustNotPage.
BLOCK TIME. The target is Robinhood Chain, where blocks are ~100 ms rather than
~12 s. Every `why` below that reasons in blocks was written against the slower
number and is now off by two orders of magnitude in the direction that matters.
The one to re-read is the immature-TWAP check: `pokeBuyback` has no cooldown, so
'per block rather than once' used to mean roughly five attempts a minute and now
means about six hundred. The check itself is unaffected — it polls the quantity
the contract branches on — but the window it is guarding is far cheaper to work
than the text implies. Cadences are wall-clock and need no adjustment.
CADENCE IS A TARGET, NOT A SCHEDULE, and the gap is wide enough to matter.
Every `cadence` below states how often the risk warrants a look. What actually
runs is .github/workflows/watch.yml, which since 2026-09-11 asks for four
passes an hour on `cron: 7,22,37,52 * * * *` and is DELIVERED about 6.5 a day.
Measure the gap against delivery, not against the cron: at ~0.27 passes an hour
the three `every 15 minutes` checks and the one `every 5 minutes` check arrive
at roughly a fourteenth and a forty-fifth of their stated rate, and `daily` is
still over-delivered. Do not correct this by shortening the cron -- measured
2026-09-13, going from hourly to every 15 minutes changed delivery from 0.27 to
0.269 passes an hour, which is to say not at all. This is recorded here rather
by editing the numbers down, because the number a risk deserves and the number
the infrastructure provides are different facts and collapsing them would lose
the first one. The consequence: this cadence cannot be relied on to bound
detection latency, and the numbers below are what it actually delivers.
AMENDED 2026-09-11: paging findings are now pushed to Telegram, so the
delivery half of that consequence is closed and 'this is not a pager' no longer
describes it. The cadence half is unchanged and is the one these numbers are
about -- GitHub delivered 27% of the passes the hourly cron asked for over 157
measured hours, so the 15-minute detection criterion is still not met, and a
check's stated interval here remains the interval it deserves rather than the
one it gets. AMENDED 2026-09-13: re-measured over 193.5 h of the 15-minute
cron at 52 of 774 passes, 7%. Observed gaps ran 2.1 h at the closest and 7.2 h
at the widest, so the latency to plan around is a ~3.3 h median. WATCHER-05
now prints that gap on every pass and pages past 8 h, which is above the widest
gap seen and therefore means 'the schedule stopped' rather than 'the schedule
is as bad as usual'.

$comment: Hook addresses are deliberately absent. There is one hook per project, so the
set is unbounded and unknowable ahead of time. Hook alerts MUST be scoped by
topic0 across all addresses, or the monitor must subscribe to LaunchCreated and
add the emitted `hook` address to its watch list. A monitor configured with a
fixed hook list silently stops covering every project created after it was set
up.
The reason no longer involves an address mask. On 4663 these were Uniswap V4
hooks and the factory mined CREATE2 salts so the address itself carried the
0x20CC permission flags; PancakeSwap Infinity reads permissions from
getHooksRegistrationBitmap() instead, so nothing is mined and hook addresses
are ordinary CREATE2 output. The conclusion is unchanged — one per project,
discovered from events — but the premise is gone, and a reader who took the
mask literally would look for a pattern in these addresses that is not there.

severities.P0: Funds at risk or governance compromised. Page immediately, 24/7. Pause the factory via the Safe. If governance itself is what is compromised, pausing may already be unavailable — announce, and tell users not to deposit.
severities.P1: Protocol-level switch thrown, or user-visible degradation. Page during waking hours; ticket otherwise.
severities.P2: Silent degradation. Ticket, review next business day.
severities.P3: Informational. Dashboard and digest only — must never page.

alerts.playbook: governance: the pending owner can still be overwritten, so do not accept. Correlate against the Safe transaction history; an authorised-but-wrong transfer is abandoned by having the owner call transferOwnership() again with the intended address. If no Safe transaction matches, the owner key is compromised.
alerts.why: Ownable2Step means a takeover needs two transactions. This is the first one, and it is the only window in which the transfer can still be abandoned by simply not accepting. Alerting on the completion instead of the start throws that window away.

alerts.playbook: governance: ownership of every platform kill switch moved. Correlate against the Safe transaction history. If nothing matches, there is no on-chain remedy left to us — announce that the factory is under unknown control and tell users not to deposit.
alerts.why: Ownership of every platform kill switch changed hands. Expected exactly twice in the system's life: once at deploy, once at the Safe handoff (PM-C2). A third occurrence is an incident until proven otherwise.

alerts.playbook: governance: ownership of the reservoir moved. Correlate against the Safe transaction history. If nothing matches, there is no on-chain remedy left to us — announce, and note that the reservoir can only be spent on buybacks, not withdrawn.
alerts.why: Same as GOV-02 for the treasury. Both contracts hand off separately, and it is entirely possible to complete one and forget the other.

alerts.playbook: governance: the pending owner can still be overwritten, so do not accept. Correlate against the Safe transaction history; an authorised-but-wrong transfer is abandoned by having the owner call transferOwnership() again with the intended address. If no Safe transaction matches, the owner key is compromised, and this is the contract holding the reservoir.
alerts.why: GOV-01 for the treasury. This entry was missing from the first draft of this file and scripts/verifyAlertTopics.js is what found it — the factory got both halves of the two-step transfer and the treasury only got the second, which would have left the abandonable window unwatched on the contract that actually holds the money.

alerts.playbook: PoG signer: whoever holds this key mints deposit quota. Correlate against the Safe transaction history. If unauthorised, pause() the factory to stop new deposits, then rotate with setPogSigner() to a key you control.
alerts.why: Whoever holds the PoG signer key can mint deposit quota. An unplanned rotation means either an incident response someone forgot to announce, or an attacker who already owns the factory.

alerts.playbook: one-shot by design, so a second occurrence means you are not talking to the contract you believe you are. Re-derive the treasury address from the deploy broadcast and confirm its runtime codehash before acting on anything else this monitor reports.
alerts.why: One-shot by design: it should fire exactly once, at deploy. A second occurrence is impossible if the contract is what we think it is, which makes it a high-value canary for 'we are not talking to the contract we believe we are'.

alerts.playbook: pause: correlate against the Safe transaction history within minutes. Ours is expected. A pause that matches no Safe transaction means the owner key is compromised — escalate to P0 and handle as governance compromise.
alerts.why: Either we did it, or someone with the owner key did. Correlate against a Safe transaction within minutes; an unmatched pause is a P0 and is handled as governance compromise, per the playbook above.

alerts.playbook: unpause: this re-opens deposits. Correlate against the Safe transaction history and confirm whatever the pause was protecting against has actually been resolved. An unpause nobody ordered escalates to P0 as governance compromise.
alerts.why: An unpause nobody ordered is worse than a pause nobody ordered: it re-opens deposits during whatever the pause was protecting against. An authorised resume has a Safe transaction behind it and a resolved cause in front of it; an unpause that can be matched to neither is handled as governance compromise, per the playbook above.

alerts.playbook: mint halt: users see the button lock within one block, so announce within 15 minutes. A zero `hook` argument is platform-wide and is a P0. The halt lapses on its own after at most 7 days, so no resume transaction is required.
alerts.why: Users see the mint button lock within one block, so the announcement clock (15 minutes) starts whether or not anyone is watching. A halt with a zero `hook` argument is platform-wide and should be treated as P0.

alerts.playbook: closes the loop on SWITCH-03: confirm the resume was intended and announce it. Absence is not a fault — a halt lapses by itself after at most 7 days.
alerts.why: Closes the loop on SWITCH-03. Absence is also meaningful: a halt lapses on its own after at most 7 days, so a resume that never arrives is expected, not a fault.

alerts.playbook: blacklist: policy requires two-engineer sign-off. Match this against the sign-off record. A blacklist with no matching record is the finding, not the blacklist itself.
alerts.why: Requires two-engineer sign-off by policy. The alert is the audit trail that proves the policy was followed; a blacklist with no matching sign-off record is the finding.

alerts.playbook: PoG cap: this is what bounds a compromised signer. Correlate against the Safe transaction history. Lowering it does not retroactively tighten hooks already deployed, because each snapshots its own perWalletCap at creation.
alerts.why: This is the cap that bounds a compromised PoG signer. Raising it widens the blast radius of GOV-04; lowering it does NOT retroactively tighten hooks already deployed, because each snapshots its own perWalletCap at creation.
Affects rounds created after it, never rounds already open. Worth a ticket so the number in the docs and the number on chain do not drift.
Pricing change. Alerting is for the audit trail, not for response.

Curation of buyback targets. The contract already refuses tokens this factory did not launch, so the abuse case is bounded — but it decides where treasury BEM goes. One thing the contract does NOT refuse is a pool younger than TWAP_WINDOW, whose buyback legs are unbounded; STATE-07 is the check for that, and this alert is where a human first sees the listing that trips it.
Counterpart to PARAM-04.

This dial IS the one-deposit-per-project rule, not a spam throttle, and this entry used to say the opposite -- that raising it was 'a soft denial of service on deposits'. Raising it is the rule: at >= DURATION_SLOW (72h) a wallet's second deposit into one project cannot fit inside the genesis window, and below that the instalment path returns. So the two directions are not symmetric and only one of them is a repeal. The event alone cannot tell 72 -> 96 from 72 -> 24, which is why this stays P2 and the conditional lives in STATE-08. Treat this as the prompt to go read what the new value is.
Switches PoG quota between a rolling window and a lifetime budget. A wider window means each attested wallet can deposit more over time, so it interacts with the PoG signer blast radius in PARAM-01.

A deliberately swallowed failure: the hook must not brick trading because the buyback engine reverted. Correct behaviour, and therefore invisible. This event is the ONLY signal that the piggyback path is broken; without an alert it degrades indefinitely with a healthy-looking dashboard.

alerts.threshold: more than 3 in 24h for the same token, or any occurrence for more than half the curated set
alerts.why: Same shape as SILENT-01, one layer down: a single broken pool is skipped so it cannot stall the batch. One skip is routine. Every token skipping means the treasury is accumulating BEM it can no longer spend, which is the one-way valve failing closed rather than open.

LIVE AGAIN, and it no longer means what the name suggests. Dormant while a missed soft cap stopped being a refund trigger; re-wired when a raise too small to carry a shelf ladder became one. Fires on the first refund() of a round whose raise could never have opened a pool, so refunds opened at genesis close rather than after the 7-day window. Not a creator failure: launch() was arithmetically impossible on this raise. LIFE-02 is the other refund reason and does accuse the creator; the two are deliberately separate events so an indexer need not guess.

Lazy-emit: fires on the first refund() of a round, not when refunds open. Means the creator never launched inside the 7-day window on a raise that COULD have opened a pool — abandonment, unlike LIFE-01, which is a round that was never launchable. Narrower than it used to be: small raises now announce as LIFE-01 and never reach this event.

Informational for humans, LOAD-BEARING for the monitor: the `hook` field is how the watch list stays current. Any monitor that scopes hook events by address must consume this and self-register. See addresses.$comment.
Normal lifecycle. Useful as the denominator for 'how many rounds launched vs failed'.

stateChecks.check: For every hook from LaunchCreated: canRefund() == true AND totalNativeDeposited > 0 AND no Refunded event yet
stateChecks.why: Nothing is emitted when refunds OPEN — refund() flips refundAnnounced lazily, on the first claimant, so a round can sit refundable and unannounced indefinitely. This is the poll that closes that gap, and it now covers both doors: the 7-day window lapsing unused, and a raise too small to carry a ladder, which opens refunds the moment genesis closes and can therefore need announcing up to a week earlier than this check used to expect. Depositors with a non-zero stake are owed a notification; a zero raise is a gap line, not a finding, because nobody is owed an exit.
stateChecks.action: Announce refund availability; tosh-status/MANUAL_INTERACTION.md §4 has the cast invocation for users who need it, and the status page already links it.

stateChecks.check: ladderTreasury BEM balance -- quoteAsset.balanceOf(treasury), NOT eth_getBalance -- is strictly non-decreasing, except across a PiggybackExecuted or BuybackBurned in the same window
stateChecks.why: The one-way valve is asserted by invariant_treasuryNeverLosesEth in test/ToshV5Invariants.t.sol against the deployed logic, but the invariant cannot speak for the deployed bytecode. This is the production-side counterpart: a balance drop with no buyback to explain it means either a withdrawal path exists or we are watching the wrong contract. NOTE THE ASSET, because getting it wrong is undetectable: the reservoir became an ERC-20 balance when the quote asset became BEM, and watch.mjs read eth_getBalance for one commit afterwards. The treasury's native balance is 0 and cannot fall, so this check passed every run while watching nothing -- it produced no error and no gap, only a clean pass. Any reimplementation against a different alerting product has to read balanceOf.
stateChecks.action: Treat as funds-at-risk: pause the factory via the Safe, then correlate the fall against buyback events and Safe transactions in the same window. A fall matching neither is a governance compromise, and once the reservoir is spent there is no on-chain remedy — announce.

stateChecks.check: factory.owner() == the expected Gnosis Safe AND factory.pendingOwner() == address(0)
stateChecks.why: Belt to GOV-01/02's braces. Event delivery can fail — a provider outage, a reorg, a misconfigured filter — and ownership is the one fact where finding out late is unacceptable. A non-zero pendingOwner is a takeover mid-flight.
stateChecks.action: Confirm the move against the Safe transaction history, and pause the factory if it was not authorised. A non-zero pendingOwner is still abandonable: have the owner call transferOwnership() again with the intended address.

stateChecks.why: Same reasoning as STATE-03 applied to GOV-04. Cheap, and it fails closed.
stateChecks.action: Correlate against the Safe transaction history. If the signer is not one we rotated to, pause() the factory to stop new deposits, then setPogSigner() to a key you control.

stateChecks.check: IF an automated keeper is configured: its wallet balance is above the gas floor. Inactive by default, because no wallet this protocol operates needs gas.
why: This check used to watch the PoG signer, on the premise that it needs gas to sign. It does not, and the premise was wrong in a way nothing downstream could catch.

registerPoG() is external and keys off msg.sender: the DEPOSITOR sends that transaction and pays for it. The signer's address appears in the contract only as the expected result of hash.recover(signature). Both consumers of the key sign without a chain connection at all — the API route uses viem's privateKeyToAccount().signMessage(), and scripts/pogSigner.ts constructs ethers.Wallet(pk) with no provider, which cannot send a transaction even in principle.

So a PoG signer holding 0 BNB signs exactly as well as one holding 50. Funding it was not merely unnecessary but slightly harmful: the key lives in a Vercel environment variable, and a key guarding a balance is worth more to steal than one guarding nothing.

The check is kept rather than deleted because the shape is right for a case that does not exist yet. pokeBuyback() is permissionless and STATE-06's remedy is currently a human calling it; automating that would introduce the protocol's first wallet that genuinely needs gas, and it would fail silently when it ran dry. Set MONITOR_KEEPER_ADDRESS at that point and this activates.

stateChecks.check: ladderTreasury BEM balance -- quoteAsset.balanceOf(treasury) -- has been >= TRIGGER_STEP (92.8 BEM, i.e. 92.8e8 base units) continuously for 24h with no PiggybackExecuted in that window
stateChecks.why: The gas gate in ToshLaunchpadHook.afterSwap skips the buyback when the triggering trade cannot afford it, which is what stops that trade from reverting. The cost is that the reservoir no longer deploys itself from trading alone: a market where wallets attach tight gas limits leaves it armed and idle, emitting NOTHING. There is deliberately no event for a skipped poke — skipping is the common case, and logging it would bill every trader for the privilege. So this has to be a balance-and-silence poll; it is the only signal that the reservoir has stopped deploying.
stateChecks.action: Call pokeBuyback() on the treasury. Permissionless — no role, no Safe transaction, any address can clear it.

stateChecks.check: For every token in ladderTokens, INDEPENDENTLY of the others: its hook's twapSqrtPriceX96() answers, and answers != 0
stateChecks.why: The buyback's anti-sandwich bound is anchored to the hook's TWAP, and the hook reports 0 for the first TWAP_WINDOW (1800s) after launch(). _buybackSqrtFloor treats 0 as 'no reference' and falls back to UNBOUNDED, so a token listed inside that window has no price bound at all, on the pool whose liquidity is thinnest. test_probeG3_immatureTwapIsRefusedAtListing measures a pool parked 1500 bps out giving up 0.93 ETH of a 3.33 ETH leg, where a matured TWAP refuses the same deviation outright; pokeBuyback has no cooldown, so it is per block rather than once. The decision to keep the unbounded fallback was taken deliberately (see _buybackSqrtFloor's natspec), which means the ONLY thing holding it shut is the operational rule not to list a young pool — and an operational rule nobody checks is not a control. This is the check. It polls the exact quantity the contract branches on rather than re-deriving the deadline from launch timestamps, so it cannot drift from the code it guards: if TWAP_WINDOW changes or maturity is redefined, this follows automatically. AMENDED 2026-09-05, on an audit re-read of this check: _buybackSqrtFloor reaches unbounded by TWO doors eight lines apart, and this check only watched one. Its catch returns the same unbounded floor when twapSqrtPriceX96() REVERTS, so a reverting hook has no bound either -- and that case used to land in the generic error handler as a hardcoded NON-PAGING record reading 'check failed', which a human parses as 'the monitor is unwell' rather than 'a listed pool has no price bound'. Worse, every read sat on one outer try, so a single throw aborted the loop and left every LATER token unchecked while naming neither the count nor the skipped indices. Both are fixed: per-token isolation, a revert pages at the same severity as a zero, an unresolvable entry names its index, and the generic handler is narrowed to the token list itself being unreadable. AMENDED 2026-09-11: addLadderToken now reads twapSqrtPriceX96() itself and reverts TwapNotMature unless it answers non-zero, so on a treasury deployed from source at or after that date NEITHER door can be entered through the listing. What changed the decision was publication rather than a new finding: this file went public with the repository, and the check and why fields below are a specification of the exploitable condition and a price list for it. The BLOCK TIME note at the head of this file is the other half of the argument -- at ~100 ms blocks, per-block means roughly six hundred attempts a minute, not five. THIS CHECK IS NOT RETIRED. AMENDED 2026-09-12: the platform was redeployed for an unrelated reason (per-project referrals), and the new treasury 0x255722226720914eF5B2CD54647f21f584BD4Ea2 is built from source carrying the gate, so the listing door IS now shut on chain — the previous version of this note said that could only arrive with a new deployment, and this is that deployment. What it did NOT buy is this check's retirement, for the reason stated immediately below: the gate fires once at listing while _buybackSqrtFloor runs on every leg, so the second door is untouched by it. Two further cautions. The gate's presence in the live treasury rests on source provenance — the deploy artefact records commit 9b9d9ce, the factory's HOOK_CREATION_CODEHASH equals this tree's keccak256(type(ToshLaunchpadHook).creationCode), and the treasury's runtime differs from this tree's build only in the 95 bytes of the poolManager immutable — and NOT on any direct observation of the gate firing, because reaching it requires a launched pool with an immature TWAP and the new factory has launched nothing yet. And the obvious shortcut for checking it does not work: TwapNotMature()'s 4-byte selector is absent from the runtime bytecode of the gated treasury, the ungated one, and this tree's own build alike, so scripts/preflightLadderListing.mjs no longer claims to read the regime off the bytecode. Separately, the gate fires once at listing while _buybackSqrtFloor runs on every leg, so a token listed with a healthy getter whose getter later reverts still buys unbounded -- the second door, which no listing-time check can see. That residual is assessed as unreachable on chain and is pre-disclosed in SECURITY.md.
stateChecks.action: Call removeLadderToken(token) on the treasury via the Safe, wait until that hook's twapSqrtPriceX96() is non-zero, then re-add. Removing does not forfeit anything — the reservoir is not spent on an unlisted token, and the window closes on the clock alone. Firing at all means the listing rule in addLadderToken's natspec was broken, so also ask why.

stateChecks.check: factory.cooldownDuration() >= DURATION_SLOW, read off hookImplementation rather than hardcoded
why: The one-deposit-per-project rule is a dial, not an invariant. It holds only while the cooldown is at least the longest genesis window: the cooldown starts no earlier than the project was created and runs at least as long as the whole window, so a second deposit has no time it could land in. Below that the instalment path returns, because the PoG quota refills every quotaWindowDuration while nativeDeposited accumulates and never resets.

That is a protocol-level switch, hence P1. README §2.2 prices it: 100 floor-sitting sybils drawing three times on a DURATION_SLOW launch reach 3.75 ETH of allocation against 2.5 ETH of gas burned, turning a 2:1 deterrent into a 1.5:1 subsidy.

⚠ Nothing else catches this on a live chain. test_cooldown_isAtLeastTheLongestGenesis pins the default in ToshFactory.sol and says nothing about what the dial was set to after deployment; setCooldownDuration is one Safe transaction, reverts nothing, and changes no screen. PARAM-06 sees the event but cannot distinguish 72 -> 96 from 72 -> 24, so the conditional has to be a state read.

It catches two different drifts with one comparison: a lowered dial, and a fourth genesis rung longer than the dial. DURATION_SLOW is read off the immutable hookImplementation for that second case -- a literal here would agree with the old world and miss it.
stateChecks.action: Call setCooldownDuration(DURATION_SLOW) on the factory via the Safe. Then check whether any genesis was open while the rule was off, and whether any wallet deposited into the same project more than once in that window -- the deposits are valid and cannot be reversed, so this is a disclosure question rather than a remediation one.

$comment: High-volume, entirely normal events. Listed explicitly because the failure mode
of a new monitoring setup is a firehose that gets muted wholesale in week two,
taking the P0 alerts down with it. Route these to a dashboard or a digest; never
to a pager.
GenesisDeposit and Deposited are the same deposit seen from the factory and from
the hook. Alerting on both double-counts every deposit.
The three tax events are per-swap and none of them may page. They are also the
revenue ledger, so how they compose matters to whoever builds the dashboard:
a BUY emits BuyTaxToTreasury AND PlatformSwapFeePaid in the same swap, carrying
70 bps and 30 bps of the BEM input respectively; a SELL emits only SellTaxBurned,
carrying the full 100 bps of the token input, because the sell leg is not split.
BuyTaxToTreasury therefore is NOT the buy-side tax total — it is the buyback
reservoir's share of it. Summing it as though it were understates the tax by 30 %
and overstates what the buyback engine received by nothing, which is the more
dangerous half of the error: the reservoir figure looks right on its own.
Platform revenue is PlatformSwapFeePaid alone, and it should never be non-zero
on a sell — if it is, the sell leg has started paying the platform in project
tokens, which the design specifically refuses.
The referral events compose the same way, and the trap is the same shape. Since
2026-09-12 the 10 % creator carve is split 8 % to the project referrer and 2 % to
a lifetime slot, so ReferralAccrued and LifetimeReferralAccrued are two legs of
ONE carve rather than two separate payouts. ReferralAccrued is therefore NOT the
referral total any more, and a dashboard carried over from before the split will
keep adding up and keep looking plausible while under-reporting by a fifth.
ProjectReferralBound is the per-project binding; ReferralBound is the lifetime
one. Both are bindings, neither moves value, and a wallet can appear in both.
